# Fuel Blends {#sec-fuel-blends}

Technologies in CIMS rarely ask for a pure fuel. A gas boiler asks for "methane", a truck for "diesel", and what arrives is a blend: mostly fossil fuel today, with some share of lower-carbon substitutes mixed in. The mix sets the fuel's cost and its lifecycle emissions. Each sector has a **fuel blend** service for each blended fuel it uses, and its technologies draw their fuel from those services. As the renewable share of a blend rises, every technology that burns it emits less, with no change to the technologies themselves.

## Blend services

| Blend | What it mixes | Sectors |
|:------|:---------------|:--------|
| Methane | Natural gas with biogas, gas from biomass gasification, renewable natural gas, and hydrogen | Every sector except Construction, Direct Air Capture, and Forestry |
| Diesel | Fossil diesel with biodiesel and renewable diesel | Every sector except Construction, Direct Air Capture, Forestry, Residential, and Waste |
| Gasoline | Fossil gasoline with ethanol | Crude Oil, Natural Gas, and both transportation sectors |
| Still gas | Fuel gas that a refinery's own units produce | Crude Oil and Petroleum Refining |
| Process gas | Gases from blast furnaces, coke ovens, and basic oxygen furnaces | Iron and Steel |

: Fuel blend services {#tbl-fuel-blends}

The first three are true blends. They mix a purchased fossil fuel with lower-carbon substitutes made in the Biofuels and Hydrogen sectors (see @sec-biofuels and @sec-hydrogen). How far a substitute can go depends on the equipment that burns the blend: many engines and burners can take only a limited share of hydrogen or ethanol without changes.

The last two aren't purchased at all. Refineries and steel mills make these gases as by-products of their own processes and burn them on site, in place of fuel they would otherwise buy. These services route the gases to the steam, reheating, and direct heat services that burn them, and CIMS counts the heat they provide at those services.

The technology database doesn't describe the blending itself; the shares and limits come from the CIMS model inputs.
